title: Interfacial polarisation and charge trapping behaviour in BiOBr/PVA polymer nanocomposite for mechanical energy harvesting and self-powered sensing applications
content: Sustainable and self-powered energy technologies are increasingly needed as eco-friendly energy sources, driving the development of triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs). In this work, bismuth oxybromide/poly(vinyl alcohol) polymer nanocomposites (BiOBr/PVA PNCs) were developed to efficiently convert mechanical energy into electrical energy for low-power electronic and sensing applications. BiOBr nanoparticles (NPs) were synthesized via a coprecipitation method and incorporated into PVA at various concentrations (0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 wt/wt%), and their structure–property correlations were evaluated. Structural analysis confirmed the tetragonal phase with the P4/nmm space group for BiOBr NPs and the successful formation of BiOBr/PVA PNCs. The vibrational bands and functional groups were confirmed through Raman and Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, respectively. Microscopic analysis revealed flower-like assemblies of ultrathin nanosheets uniformly distributed throughout the polymer matrix. Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) analysis further revealed the surface potential and work-function characteristics of the BiOBr/PVA PNCs, providing insights into their interfacial charge-transfer behaviour. Optical and photoluminescence studies demonstrated modified electronic states and interfacial interactions upon BiOBr incorporation into PVA. Dielectric studies showed enhanced polarization and charge storage behaviour. The 2.0 wt/wt% TENG demonstrated the highest voltage and current of 220 V and 21 µA, respectively, which are almost 2 times greater than those of pristine PVA (100 V, 11 µA), owing to its interfacial polarisation and prolonged charge retention. The optimised BiOBr/PVA TENG was applied for powering 50 blue LEDs and charging a capacitor with different capacities, demonstrating its potential for sustainable energy conversion. Furthermore, the device was employed as a self-powered sensing system capable of distinguishing different finger tapping modes through different voltage responses, making it suitable as a sustainable self-powered energy harvester and sensing device.
